summary: Presents two methods for achieving low-latency handoffs in Mobile IPv4, along with a combination of them. Handoffs between foreign agents can take too long for real-time or delay-sensitive services, and these methods aim to shorten that delay. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Switching from one Wi-Fi spot to another can cause a pause, which is bad for phone calls. This note offers tricks to make the switch quicker.

subtitle: Techniques to minimize handoff latency for real-time applications in Mobile IPv4.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv4 handoffs between foreign agents can take too long for delay-sensitive services like phone calls because the mobile node must wait for the underlying layer 2 handoff to complete before starting layer 3 registration.
tldr.mechanism: Two complementary techniques use layer 2 triggers to begin registration before or after the layer 2 connection switches: PRE-REGISTRATION allows the mobile node to register with the new foreign agent while still connected to the old one; POST-REGISTRATION sets up a tunnel to forward traffic immediately while registration completes in the background.
tldr.outcome: Handoff latency and packet loss are significantly reduced, enabling support for real-time services over Mobile IPv4, though deployment depends on specific wireless technologies.

today: RFC 4881 is an Experimental protocol for low-latency handoffs in Mobile IPv4. It has not been obsoleted, and implementers interested in supporting real-time services over Mobile IPv4 may apply these techniques, the effectiveness of which depends on the specific wireless technology in use.

sections.title: The Handoff Latency Problem
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 allows mobile nodes to maintain connectivity while moving between subnets served by different foreign agents. However, the handoff process introduces delays that exceed the threshold tolerated by delay-sensitive applications such as voice calls or video conferences. The RFC addresses this by presenting two techniques and their combination to minimize the handoff latency.

The fundamental problem stems from the strict separation between layer 2 (L2, the wireless connection) and layer 3 (L3, the IP registration). A mobile node can only communicate with a foreign agent after completing its L2 handoff, and the L3 registration process takes non-zero time. During this period, the mobile node cannot send or receive IP packets, causing service interruption.
sections.eli5: When you move between rooms with Wi-Fi, your phone must finish connecting to the new Wi-Fi, then tell the network 'I moved.' During these steps, calls drop. This document explains how to shorten that dead time.

sections.title: Low-Latency Handoff Techniques
sections.content:
The RFC describes three techniques: PRE-REGISTRATION, POST-REGISTRATION, and a combined approach. PRE-REGISTRATION allows a mobile node to start registering with the new foreign agent (nFA) before completing the layer 2 handoff from the old foreign agent (oFA), either initiated by the mobile node or by the network. POST-REGISTRATION allows the old and new foreign agents to set up a temporary tunnel that forwards traffic to the mobile node at its new location, enabling immediate service while the formal registration completes in the background.

The techniques rely on layer 2 triggers, which are signals from the wireless link layer that inform the IP layer of handoff events. These triggers can occur at the mobile node, the old foreign agent, or the new foreign agent, and inform the respective entity of movement before or after the layer 2 connection changes.
sections.eli5: PRE method: prepare your bag and buy tickets at the new destination before leaving the old one. POST method: have someone at the old place forward your mail to the new place immediately. Combined: do both, and whichever finishes first wins.

sections.title: Layer 2 Triggers and Movement Detection
sections.content:
Layer 2 triggers are technology-agnostic signals that abstract wireless-specific information. The RFC defines several trigger types: an L2-MT (mobile trigger) at the mobile node indicating movement to a specific new foreign agent; an L2-ST (source trigger) at the old foreign agent indicating that a layer 2 handoff is about to occur; an L2-TT (target trigger) at the new foreign agent indicating an incoming handoff; an L2-LU (link-up) trigger signaling that the L2 connection is established; and an L2-LD (link-down) trigger at the old foreign agent indicating the L2 connection is lost.

Different wireless technologies provide these triggers at different times and to different entities. Some wireless links provide advance triggers well before handoff, while others provide little or no advance notice. The RFC's techniques accommodate this variability by using different trigger types for different scenarios, allowing operators to optimize for their specific wireless technology.
sections.eli5: Different Wi-Fi systems warn you about moving at different times: some say 'you are about to lose signal,' others just disconnect. The techniques work with whatever warning your network gives.

sections.title: The PRE-REGISTRATION Handoff Method
sections.content:
PRE-REGISTRATION allows the mobile node to perform registration with the new foreign agent while still connected to the old one. When the mobile node receives an L2-MT (mobile trigger) containing the identifier of the new foreign agent, or when the old foreign agent receives an L2-ST (source trigger), the mobile node can begin soliciting and processing router advertisements from the new foreign agent to obtain a new care-of address. The mobile node then sends a registration request to the new foreign agent through the old foreign agent.

Network-initiated PRE-REGISTRATION can also occur when the new foreign agent receives an L2-TT (target trigger) and proactively sends a router advertisement tunnel to the mobile node through the old foreign agent. The mobile node can prepare its registration message before the layer 2 handoff completes. Once the layer 2 handoff is complete, the mobile node can immediately activate the prepared registration, achieving near-instantaneous layer 3 connectivity.
sections.eli5: You prepare your exit plan at the old location and your arrival plan at the new location while still connected to the old Wi-Fi. When you switch, you are already set up at the new place.

sections.title: The POST-REGISTRATION Handoff Method
sections.content:
POST-REGISTRATION uses a temporary bidirectional tunnel (BET) between the old foreign agent (oFA) and new foreign agent (nFA) to forward traffic immediately after the layer 2 handoff, before the formal layer 3 registration completes. When the old foreign agent receives an L2-ST (source trigger) or when the new foreign agent receives an L2-TT (target trigger), the two agents can exchange Handoff Request (HRqst) and Handoff Reply (HRply) messages to establish the tunnel.

Once the tunnel is active, traffic destined for the mobile node is forwarded from the old foreign agent to the new foreign agent, and the mobile node can receive packets immediately upon connecting to the new network. The mobile node then performs a formal Mobile IPv4 registration when ready, which may be delayed from the layer 2 handoff. This provides low-loss and low-latency handoff without requiring the mobile node's immediate involvement in registration signaling.
sections.eli5: The two Wi-Fi routers create a direct connection: the old one forwards your packets to the new one as soon as you switch. You can then do paperwork (register) whenever convenient.

sections.title: Combined Handoff Method
sections.content:
The combined method runs PRE-REGISTRATION and POST-REGISTRATION in parallel. If the PRE-REGISTRATION handoff completes before the layer 2 handoff is done, the result is seamless connectivity with the minimal latency of PRE-REGISTRATION. If PRE-REGISTRATION does not complete within a technology-dependent timeout, the old foreign agent starts forwarding traffic via POST-REGISTRATION as a backup mechanism. This hybrid approach provides robustness: the mobile node benefits from the low-latency PRE method when possible, but falls back to the low-loss POST method if registration takes too long.

The combined method is particularly valuable for wireless technologies where the timing of layer 2 handoff events is unpredictable. It ensures that real-time services experience minimal disruption regardless of whether the mobile node can complete registration before or after the layer 2 handoff.
sections.eli5: Try to be ready before switching (PRE), but if that takes too long, start with the backup tunnel (POST). Either way, you stay connected.
